sections.heading: Coming to you in my weakness
sections.text: Lord, you know how unfit I feel to serve you right now. My heart feels dull and cold. I do not have strength in myself to do anything that truly honors you. I am weak, limited, and easily distracted, and when I look honestly at myself, I have no reason to be proud.
theological_themes: Human weakness and inability apart from God
Dependence on grace for any fruitful service

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that apart from him his disciples can do nothing of lasting spiritual fruitfulness. This grounds the prayer’s confession that service for God cannot come from self-reliance.
Paul says that our sufficiency is not from ourselves but from God. That directly supports asking God for the ability to serve him rather than pretending to possess it naturally.

sections.heading: Naming the coldness and sin I feel
sections.text: I do not even know what you want from me next, and I feel painfully far from you. I know you have not stopped being faithful, but I sense your nearness so little. You are making me face sins I would rather forget, and the deeper sinfulness that runs through me. It feels as if sin has stained every part of me—my thoughts, motives, desires, and actions.
theological_themes: Spiritual dryness and felt distance from God
Conviction of past sins and indwelling sin
The pervasive corruption of sin in human nature

scripture_references.connection: David confesses not only particular acts of sin but a deeper sinfulness rooted in his nature. This helps express the prayer’s awareness that the problem is not merely occasional failure but corruption within.

Paul describes the painful conflict of wanting what is good while still finding sin close at hand. The passage gives biblical language for the distress of a believer who feels the weight of indwelling sin.

sections.heading: Asking for grace that changes me
sections.text: Please come to me again with the kind of grace that wakes a sinner up and turns the heart back to you. I have heard the gospel and still treated your mercy lightly; forgive me. Make my soul long for holiness. Give me a steady, whole-hearted devotion to you. Let your grace grow in me more and more, not just in words or feelings, but in real change every day.
theological_themes: Need for renewing and converting grace
Longing for holiness and growth in grace

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes grace not only as pardon but as power that trains believers to renounce sin and live godly lives. That supports asking for grace that produces practical holiness.
Peter commands believers to grow in the grace and knowledge of Christ. This connects with the prayer’s longing for daily increase in grace rather than spiritual stagnation.

sections.heading: Depending on you to keep me near
sections.text: Father, I feel lost in the very thing I most want—to belong to you fully and live close to you. I am discouraged because I fall so far short of what I desire. Please keep me going a little longer. Hold me until the hour of rescue you have appointed. I cannot even lift my heart to you unless, in your kindness, you bring me near.
theological_themes: Dependence on divine mercy from beginning to end

scripture_references.connection: The psalmist admits that heart and flesh may fail, yet God remains his strength and portion. This fits the prayer’s cry for God to sustain a failing, discouraged heart.
Jesus says that no one comes to him unless the Father draws him. This supports the confession that even drawing near to God depends on God’s gracious initiative.
Paul’s confidence is that God finishes the good work he began in his people. That gives biblical hope to the request to be kept until final deliverance.

sections.heading: Learning watchfulness, humility, and faithful service
sections.text: Make me humble, careful, and tender-hearted. Keep me alert so I do not grieve or dishonor my dearest Friend, Jesus, in what I think, say, or do. I trust you and lean on you; I need you at every moment to help me and lead me. Let even my fears, struggles, and distress become Christ’s classroom for me. Teach me humility there, and make me more useful for whatever service you give me.
theological_themes: Reliance on God’s leading and help
Affliction as Christ’s training in humility and usefulness

scripture_references.connection: Jesus tells his disciples to watch and pray because the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak. This supports the prayer’s desire to be alert and dependent so as not to fall into sin.
James calls believers to humility before God and promises grace to the humble. This grounds the prayer’s request that distress would teach lowliness rather than pride or despair.
Paul learns that Christ’s power is displayed in weakness. This supports the hope that personal weakness and distress can become preparation for more faithful service.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original’s statement that every motion is sin could be misunderstood as denying that any real good can be worked in a believer by the Holy Spirit. I rendered it as sin staining every part of the person—consistent with total depravity and indwelling sin—without implying that grace is absent or ineffective.

The phrase about feeling deserted by God is spiritually intense. I preserved the felt distance while clarifying that God has not ceased to be faithful, to avoid confusing subjective spiritual dryness with actual abandonment by God.

The original’s 'happy hour of deliverance' may refer to relief from the present inward trial, final deliverance at death, or ultimate salvation at Christ’s return. I kept the wording broad as 'the hour of rescue you have appointed.'
significant_interpretive_choices: I interpreted 'gospel-abusing sinner' as a confession of treating gospel mercy lightly while continuing in sin, rather than as rejection of the gospel itself.

I rendered 'Christ’s school' as 'Christ’s classroom' to preserve the concrete image of suffering and distress as a place where Christ teaches humility, while making the phrase natural in contemporary speech.
I kept the prayer in first person singular throughout because the metadata identifies it as a private personal prayer.
